about.title: Alameda Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: An injury at work rarely arrives with a clear explanation of what happens next. In Alameda, that might mean a fall from scaffolding on a Park Street storefront renovation, a back strain in a warehouse, or a collision while making deliveries along Lincoln Avenue or Central Avenue. Public records show 129 injury collisions in the city during 2025, with 166 people hurt, a reminder that driving is part of many jobs here. California handles work injuries in two lanes. Workers' compensation covers medical care and partial wage replacement through your employer's insurer, no matter who was at fault, and it is usually the only claim you can bring against the employer itself. Separately, if someone outside your company contributed to the injury, a subcontractor, a property owner, an equipment manufacturer, or another driver, you may also have a personal injury claim against that third party. We handle Alameda workplace injury claims on a contingency basis, meaning no fee unless there is a recovery.

items.title: Two Paths, Clearly Explained
items.desc: Workers' comp is usually your only remedy against your employer, but a negligent subcontractor, property owner, equipment maker, or driver can open a separate claim. We can sort out which applies to your Alameda injury.

items.title: Deadlines Kept in View
items.desc: You have 30 days to report an injury to your employer, and any third-party claim generally carries California's two-year deadline. Reaching out early keeps both clocks from working against you.

items.title: Protection Against Retaliation
items.desc: California law forbids your employer from punishing you for reporting an injury or filing a claim. If your hours were cut or your job threatened after you spoke up, that is worth raising with us.

items.question: I was hit while driving for work on Lincoln Avenue in Alameda. Is that a workers' comp case or a car accident case?
items.answer: It can be both. Because you were on the job, workers' comp should cover your medical care and part of your lost wages regardless of who caused the crash. If the other driver was at fault, you may also have a separate personal injury claim against that driver, which is where we can add real value.

items.question: What happens if I didn't report my injury to my employer right away?
items.answer: California asks you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days, so do it as soon as you can, in writing if possible. Missing the window can complicate a workers' comp claim, though it does not always end it. We can review your timeline and tell you where you stand.

items.question: Does it cost anything to contact us or to discuss my case with an attorney?
items.answer: No. There is no cost for a free case review. We handle injury claims on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery.
